title: Christian Leadership
summary: Leading like Jesus in church, ministry, work and community: the servant leader's character, vision and planning, building teams, handling conflict and finishing well.
description: Leadership is influence used for God's purposes. This course draws on Scripture and the lives of Moses, Nehemiah, David, Jesus and Paul to teach the character of a servant leader, how to discern and share vision, plan and organise, build and develop teams, make decisions, handle conflict and criticism, manage time and money with integrity, and finish well.
objectives: Define Christian leadership as servant influence
Develop the character required for godly leadership
Cast vision, plan and organise like Nehemiah
Build, delegate to and develop teams
Handle conflict and criticism, and finish well
outcomes: Identify character qualities and pitfalls of leaders
Write a simple vision and action plan
Respond to conflict and criticism biblically

modules.title: Servant Leadership
modules.intro: Jesus redefined leadership as service. This week we study what Christian leadership is.

lessons.title: Not so among you
lessons.body:
"Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them... But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:42-45).

Christian leadership is **influence used to serve God's purposes and people**, not a position to gain status, money or control.

Jesus washed feet (John 13:14-15). A leader's question is not "How can they serve me?" but "How can I serve them toward God's purpose?"

lessons.title: Called and gifted
lessons.body:
God calls leaders: Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3), Gideon threshing wheat (Judges 6), David the shepherd boy (1 Samuel 16), Peter the fisherman (Luke 5).

Often God chooses unlikely people: "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1 Corinthians 1:27). Moses protested, "I am slow of speech" (Exodus 4:10); God promised, "I will be with thy mouth".

Leadership is also a gift: "he that ruleth, with diligence" (Romans 12:8). Leaders serve in families, churches, schools, businesses and governments. Every believer leads someone and influences others.

lessons.title: Leading under authority
lessons.body:
Christian leaders are themselves under authority: Christ's (Colossians 1:18), Scripture's, and often other human leaders. The centurion understood authority: "I also am a man set under authority" (Matthew 8:9).

Leaders will give account: those who "watch for your souls, as they that must give account" (Hebrews 13:17). Stewards must be faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2).

Saul lost his kingdom when he disobeyed God to please the people (1 Samuel 15:22-24). David, though anointed, refused to seize power by killing Saul (1 Samuel 24:6). Godly leaders wait for God's timing and submit to His will.

terms.def: Influence that moves people toward a shared purpose.
Leading by serving others toward God's purposes, after Jesus' example.
God's summons to a particular task or role.
A Spirit-given ability to lead with diligence (Romans 12:8).
Being accountable to God and to appropriate human leaders.
Leadership as a trust for which we must give account.

texts.teaches: The Son of man came not to be served but to serve.
You also ought to wash one another's feet.
God chose the weak things to confound the mighty.
He that ruleth, with diligence.
To obey is better than sacrifice.

summary: Christian leadership is servant influence, not status.
God calls and equips unlikely people.
Leaders are under authority and will give account.
Obedience to God matters more than pleasing people.

questions.q: What did Jesus say the great among you must be?
What did Moses say when God called him?
Why did Saul lose his kingdom?
options: He disobeyed God to please the people

modules.title: The Leader's Character
modules.intro: Character is the foundation of lasting leadership. This week we study the qualities and pitfalls of leaders.

lessons.title: Integrity and humility
lessons.body:
"The integrity of the upright shall guide them" (Proverbs 11:3). Samuel could ask the nation, "Whose ox have I taken?... or whom have I defrauded?" and they answered, "Thou hast not defrauded us" (1 Samuel 12:3-4). Daniel's enemies could find no fault (Daniel 6:4).

**Humility**: Moses "was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth" (Numbers 12:3). "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble" (James 4:6).

Humble leaders admit mistakes, give credit to others, receive correction and do not need to be the centre. Integrity means being the same person in private and public.

lessons.title: Faith, courage and diligence
lessons.body:
God told Joshua, "Be strong and of a good courage... for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Joshua 1:9). Leaders must make hard decisions and face opposition.

Nehemiah combined faith and diligence: "We made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night" (Nehemiah 4:9).

Leaders must also be **teachable** and keep growing, **disciplined** in time and habits, and **loving** toward those they lead. Paul's charge: "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. Let all your things be done with charity" (1 Corinthians 16:13-14).

lessons.title: Pitfalls of leaders
lessons.body:
Scripture records leaders who fell:

- **Pride**: Uzziah grew strong, then "his heart was lifted up to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:16).
- **Sexual sin**: David with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11).
- **Greed**: Gehazi took Naaman's gifts and was struck with leprosy (2 Kings 5:20-27).
- **Jealousy and insecurity**: Saul's jealousy of David (1 Samuel 18:7-9).
- **Isolation and burnout**: Elijah alone under a tree (1 Kings 19).
- **Abuse of power**: Rehoboam's harshness split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:13-16).

Safeguards: accountability, honest friends, a strong devotional life, transparency with money, and rest.

terms.def: Wholeness and consistency of character in public and private.
A right view of oneself before God, free from pride.
Strength to do right despite fear or opposition.
Willingness to learn and receive correction.
Exhaustion from prolonged overwork and stress.
Openness, especially in finances and decisions.

texts.teaches: The integrity of the upright shall guide them.
God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.
Be strong and of good courage; God is with you.
When Uzziah was strong, his heart was lifted up to destruction.
Let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.

summary: Integrity and humility are foundations of leadership.
Leaders need faith, courage, diligence and love.
Pride, sexual sin, greed, jealousy and burnout destroy leaders.
Accountability and a strong walk with God are safeguards.

questions.q: Who was described as very meek above all men?
What split the kingdom under Rehoboam?

modules.title: Vision, Planning and Teams
modules.intro: Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls in 52 days. This week we learn vision, planning and teamwork from him and others.

lessons.title: Vision from God
lessons.body:
Nehemiah heard of Jerusalem's broken walls and "wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed" (Nehemiah 1:4). Vision began with a burden and prayer.

He then shared the vision clearly: "Ye see the distress that we are in... come, and let us build up the wall" (2:17). He linked it to God's hand on him (2:18), and the people said, "Let us rise up and build."

A vision is a clear picture of a better future God wants. "Write the vision, and make it plain" (Habakkuk 2:2). Good vision is God-centred, specific, shared and worth sacrifice.

lessons.title: Planning and organising
lessons.body:
Nehemiah planned carefully: he asked the king for time, letters and timber (2:5-8); he inspected the walls by night before announcing plans (2:12-15); he assigned families to sections near their own homes (chapter 3).

Faith and planning go together: "The preparations of the heart in man... from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:1); "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established" (16:3).

A simple plan answers: What is the goal? What steps are needed? Who will do each? What resources? By when? How will we know we have succeeded? Review and adjust as you go (Proverbs 15:22).

lessons.title: Building and developing teams
lessons.body:
Moses was wearing himself out judging the people alone. Jethro said, "The thing that thou doest is not good... thou art not able to perform it thyself alone" (Exodus 18:17-18). He advised choosing "able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness" and delegating (18:21-22).

Good delegation gives clear responsibility and authority, trains people, trusts them, supports them and reviews progress.

Jesus developed the Twelve; Paul trained Timothy and Titus. Leaders should always be raising the next generation (2 Timothy 2:2). A team with diverse gifts achieves more than one gifted person (1 Corinthians 12:14-21; Ecclesiastes 4:9).

terms.def: A clear picture of a better future that God wants.
A deep, God-given concern that moves to prayer and action.
Deciding goals, steps, people, resources and timing.
Giving others responsibility and authority for parts of the work.
Preparing future leaders to carry on the work.
A group with diverse gifts working toward a shared goal.

texts.teaches: Nehemiah wept, mourned, fasted and prayed.
They said, Let us rise up and build.
Write the vision and make it plain.
Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans shall be established.
You are not able to perform it yourself alone.

summary: Vision begins with a burden and prayer, then is shared clearly.
Nehemiah planned carefully and organised the people.
Delegate to capable, godly people and develop future leaders.

questions.q: What did Nehemiah do when he heard about Jerusalem?
How did Nehemiah assign work on the wall?
options: Families built sections near their homes

questions.q: What qualities did Jethro say leaders should have?

modules.title: Conflict, Criticism and Finishing Well
modules.intro: Every leader faces opposition. This week we study conflict, criticism, decisions and finishing well.

lessons.title: Handling opposition and criticism
lessons.body:
Nehemiah faced mockery (4:1-3), threats (4:8), distraction (6:2-3) and false rumours (6:5-8). He prayed, guarded, kept working and refused to be drawn away: "I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down" (6:3).

When criticised, ask: Is any of this true? Take it to God, learn from valid criticism (Proverbs 12:1), and do not retaliate. Moses was criticised by Miriam and Aaron and left it to God (Numbers 12).

David encouraged himself in the LORD when his own men spoke of stoning him (1 Samuel 30:6). Leaders need a secure identity in God, not in people's approval (Galatians 1:10).

lessons.title: Conflict and decisions
lessons.body:
Conflict is normal. Paul and Barnabas had "sharp contention" over Mark and parted (Acts 15:39), yet later Paul valued Mark (2 Timothy 4:11).

The Jerusalem council modelled good conflict resolution: the issue was stated, all sides heard, Scripture consulted, a decision made and communicated clearly and kindly (Acts 15:6-31).

For decisions: gather facts, pray, consult Scripture and wise counsel (Proverbs 15:22), consider those affected, decide, communicate clearly and review. Abigail's wise, quick intervention prevented David's revenge (1 Samuel 25). Leaders should be peacemakers (Matthew 5:9).

lessons.title: Finishing well
lessons.body:
Many leaders start well but finish poorly: Solomon's heart turned away in old age (1 Kings 11:4). Others finish well: Paul could say, "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7). Joshua and Samuel ended with integrity.

To finish well: keep a fresh walk with God; stay accountable; keep learning; guard family; handle money transparently; prepare successors and hand over gracefully, as Moses did to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7-8) and Elijah to Elisha.

The aim is to hear, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" (Matthew 25:21).

terms.def: Resistance to a leader or work, from inside or outside.
Correction that helps a leader improve.
Handling disagreements fairly and peacefully.
Advice from godly, experienced people (Proverbs 15:22).
Remaining faithful to God to the end of one's life and leadership.
Passing leadership to a prepared successor.

texts.teaches: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.
David encouraged himself in the LORD his God.
In the multitude of counsellors purposes are established.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course.
Well done, thou good and faithful servant.

summary: Respond to opposition with prayer, vigilance and focus.
Learn from criticism without retaliating; find security in God.
Resolve conflict fairly, as at the Jerusalem council.
Finish well and hand over gracefully.

questions.q: What did Nehemiah say to those trying to distract him?
options: I am doing a great work and cannot come down

questions.q: Whom did Paul and Barnabas disagree about?
Who finished poorly as his heart turned away in old age?
To whom did Moses hand over leadership?

short.q: What is servant leadership, according to Mark 10:42-45?
short.model: Unlike rulers who lord it over others, Christian leaders serve, following the Son of man who came to serve and give His life.

short.q: Name three character qualities of godly leaders.
Name three pitfalls of leaders with biblical examples.
What can we learn about vision from Nehemiah?
short.model: Vision begins with a burden and prayer, is shared clearly, and points to God's hand at work.

short.q: What principles of delegation come from Exodus 18?
short.model: No leader can do everything alone; choose able, God-fearing, truthful, unselfish people and give them real responsibility.

short.q: How can a leader finish well?
short.model: Keep a fresh walk with God, stay accountable, guard family and money, and prepare successors.

lists.q: List four biblical leaders and one lesson from each.
List four questions a simple plan should answer.

assignments.title: A vision and plan
assignments.prompt: Identify a need in your church, fellowship or community. Using Nehemiah 1-6, write a vision statement and a simple action plan (goal, steps, people, resources, timeline, measures), with biblical reasons for your approach.

assignments.title: A leader study
assignments.prompt: Study the life of one biblical leader (for example Moses, Nehemiah, David or Paul). Describe their calling, strengths, failures, how they handled opposition, and whether they finished well. Draw five lessons for leaders today.

reading: John C. Maxwell, The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership
Henry and Richard Blackaby, Spiritual Leadership
